newsitem.title: USA: Florida says homeowners denied insurance discounts.
newsitem.headline: Florida says homeowners denied insurance discounts.

text.p: Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson said Friday that leading insurers were shortchanging or denying Florida homeowners legally required discounts on insurance policies.

Nelson repeated at a news conference that he would approve no rate hikes from home insurers until each had proven that it was fully complying with Florida requirements that homeowners be given discounts for hurricane shutters, strict building-code enforcement and higher deductibles.
"This is inexcusable, and enough is enough," Nelson said. "We are tightening the screws."

Homeowner insurance in south Florida has doubled since 1992, when Hurricane Andrew left $16 billion in insured losses. Premiums for home insurance have risen an estimated 80 percent across all of Florida.

The losses left 11 insurers insolvent, caused an exodus of several insurers from Florida markets and spurred creation of a joint underwriting association (JUA) to cover homeowners unable to get coverage elsewhere.
Some 700,000 Floridians are enrolled in the JUA, and Nelson a month ago refused permission for the JUA to raise it rates an average 5.3 percent.

Nelson said a study commissioned by his Department of Insurance had shown wide variations on discounts required by laws passed in 1995 and 1996. The laws require discounts for homeowners who buy supplemental policies against wind damage and for other reasons.

Most of the 20 leading home insurers in Florida give policyholders only a two percent premium discount for installing window and door shutters, according to the study. But an insurance rating group suggests shutter discounts range from five to 18 percent, Nelson said.
Only Allstate Insurance Co gives a discount to owners of new homes located in towns with strict building-code enforcement, Nelson said. Such a discount could be as much as 11 percent.
In Franklin County, Fla., insurers give discounts ranging from 10 to 71 percent of homeowners who buy separate policies covering damages from winds, according to the study.
But, Nelson said, all the discounts should be about 70 percent.

Only six of the companies offer discounts for homeowners willing to accept deductibles equaling two percent of the value of their properties for damages from hurricanes, even though all have been required to do so since January 1.
The study noted that not all the insurers are currently required to offer the discounts, since some discounts are cued to rate filings yet to be made.

The Florida study also covered policies offered by State Farm Fire & Casualty, Nationwide Mutual Fire Insurance Co, United Services Automobile Association, Prudential Property & Casualty, Standard Fire Insurance, Metropolitan Property, Auto Insurance of Hartford and Liberty Mutual Fire Insurance Co.

The others covered were: Florida Farm Bureau General Insurance Co, Federal Insurance Co, Auto Owners Insurance Co, USAA Casualty Insurance Co, First Floridian Auto & Home Standard, Government Employees Insurance Co, Hartford Insurance Co of the Midwest, Fireman's Fund Insurance Co, Florida Farm Bureau Casualty Insurance Co, First Floridian Auto & Home Preferred and State Farm General Insurance Co.
